decisions.quote: In the ﬁrst part of the paper, we replicate past work, showing that trends in the demand for redistribution among Americans has been largely ﬂat or perhaps slightly negative over the last four decades. We show that this result is robust across different redistributive questions as well as different data sets.
decisions.reason: The study tests whether the previously reported flat trend in redistribution demand holds across different survey datasets (GSS and ANES), additional survey waves through 2012, and alternative survey measures, rather than merely re-analyzing a single original dataset.

decisions.quote: Kenworthy, Lane, and Leslie McCall. 2008. “Inequality, Public Opinion and Redistribution.” Socio-Economic Review 6, no. 1: 35–68.
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row (using the 2007 online-first publication year for DOI 10.1093/ser/mwm006) and blind target 1 (using the 2008 print year in the reference list) identify the same paper by Kenworthy and McCall.

decisions.quote: Across the four measures, we are able to replicate the ﬁnding of previous literature showing no increase in support for redistribution over this period of increased inequality.
decisions.reason: Because the study is a replication and the authors explicitly conclude that they replicate the prior finding of no increase in support for redistribution during rising inequality, the shipped outcome 'successful' is correct.

decisions.location: Introduction, p. 368, lines 56-60 (and Section I / I.A, pp. 371-375, Figure 2; References, p. 404)
decisions.quote:
In reality, demand for
income redistribution in the United States has remained ﬂat by some mea-
sures and decreased according to others (see Kuziemko and others 2013),
as we document later in this paper.
decisions.reason: Ashok, Kuziemko, and Washington (2015) cite Kuziemko et al. (2013, NBER WP 18865; linked as one report family in References, p. 404, to its revised 2015 American Economic Review article, 105(4): 1478–1508) for the flat/decreasing U.S. redistribution-demand trend (p. 368) and re-estimate it in Section I / I.A (pp. 371–375, Figure 2), distinct from shipped row 2155 (Kenworthy & McCall, 2007/2008). Both the 2013 NBER working paper (p. 1; Figure 1, p. 33) and the 2015 AER article (p. 1479, Figure 1) empirically plot historical GSS 8 - eqwlth responses since 1978, separate from their mTurk experiments. However, visual inspection of both Figure 1s shows that 2013 NBER Figure 1 ends at 2010, whereas 2015 AER Figure 1 extends to 2012 with visibly different points and fits; neither version states endpoints, GSS weights, or exclusions in text, captions, or appendix. In Section I.A, Ashok et al. analyze GSS eqwlth (weighted by wtssall * oversamp, excluding spanint = 2) using a preferred pre-recession fit through 2006 (a subset of both originals' historical waves, framed on p. 371 as checking that patterns are not driven by data or coding differences) and a full-sample fit through 2012. Relative to 2013 NBER Figure 1 (ending 2010), the 2012 wave is new data (replication); relative to 2015 AER Figure 1 (ending 2012), no post-2012 wave is added (reproduction). Because contemporaneous 2015 publication and bibliography linkage do not establish analysis chronology or identical GSS observations/weights, record_type (replication vs. reproduction) remains genuinely version-specific ambiguous.
